title: Socket pacing and proxy throttling labbook
content:
Purpose and quick summary:

This labbook documents a focused set of experiments to understand how socket-level pacing interacts with L7 proxies during token-streamed responses (inference streaming). The goal was to reproduce and measure egress microbursts, quantify tail-latency amplification from proxy buffering, and test mitigations that keep median latency low while avoiding token drop/regression for KV-cache warmups.

High-level findings (TL;DR):
- Uncoordinated small writes from the runtime cause microbursts that a downstream proxy (envoy/nginx L7) amplifies into 99.9th percentile spikes when the proxy applies fixed-size buffers or per-connection drain timers.
- Application-level pacing (coalescing to ~2–4 KB frames at the socket layer, with time budget ~4–8ms) reduced 99th/99.9th latency by 25–60% on our testbed for single-token steady streaming workloads, with <2% token-per-second throughput loss.
- Kernel and TLS interactions (Nagle, TCP_CORK, TLS record coalescing) matter: disabling Nagle (TCP_NODELAY) alone improved first-byte but increased microburst pressure downstream; pairing TCP_NODELAY with application pacing gave best overall p99 and p999 profiles.
- Proxy config knobs that helped: stream window throttling, max-buffered-bytes per stream, and drain-timeout tuning. In some cases, lowering proxy per-stream buffer prevented head-of-line amplification.

Testbed and harness:
- Hardware: 2x c6i.4xlarge-like instances (client, backend) connected through a proxy node (envoy) in the same AZ. NICs 25 Gbps simulated with tc shaping for controlled packetization and egress delays.
- Backend: minimal HTTP/2 server that speaks gRPC and plain HTTP chunked streaming; our serving runtime process runs a stub inference model that emits tokens at configurable inter-token intervals and token sizes.
- Clients: 200 concurrent connections (emulated), each sequentially requesting a streaming generation; load generator implemented in Go to control flush patterns precisely.
- Metrics collected: per-request latency (first token, median, p90/p95/p99/p999), socket write syscall patterns (size, timestamp), kernel TCP retransmits, TLS record sizes (via s2n/OpenSSL trace), pprof CPU profiles, and eBPF traces for syscall scheduling and packet drops.

Workloads and variables:
- Token emission patterns: steady 1-token-per-5ms (simulated interactive), bursty 3-tokens-at-once, and KV-cache warmup (first N tokens cold vs warm).
- Chunking strategies tested:
  1) No coalescing (write each token immediately)
  2) Small coalesce (accumulate ~512–1024 bytes or 3–5ms)
  3) Mid coalesce (2–4 KB or 6–12ms)
  4) Large coalesce / flush once per 50ms
- Socket/TCP toggles: TCP_NODELAY on/off, TCP_CORK on/off, SO_SNDBUF tuning (16KB..512KB), explicit rate pacing using a userland timer vs kernel pacing (SO_MAX_PACING_RATE where supported).
- Proxy configs: default buffering, reduced per-stream max-buffered-bytes, disabled automatic flush to client on drain, drain-timeout adjusted (10ms..200ms), and HTTP/2 SETTINGS adjustments (initial window size, max concurrent streams).

Selected results (representative):
- No coalescing + proxy-default: p50=12ms, p95=38ms, p99=210ms, p999=1.1s. Observed many small writes (~200–600 bytes) at 1–3ms spacing; proxy buffered and then flushed in 15–30KB bursts during its drain window, producing egress microbursts and queueing delays at the egress NIC.
- Small coalesce (512–1KB, 4ms): p50=14ms, p95=34ms, p99=140ms, p999=420ms. Microbursts reduced; some increased median due to deliberate buffering, but p999 reduced substantially.
- Mid coalesce (2–4KB, 8ms) + TCP_NODELAY: p50=16ms, p95=28ms, p99=95ms, p999=210ms. Best p99/p999 win with modest median cost.
- Large coalesce (50ms flush): p50=45ms, p95=160ms, p99=520ms, p999=1.8s. Too coarse for interactive SLOs.
- Kernel pacing (SO_MAX_PACING_RATE) + small coalesce: similar p99 to mid coalesce but more stable across packet drop experiments; adding kernel pacing reduced retransmit-induced p999 outliers.

Instrumentation notes and surprising observations:
- eBPF socket timestamps reveal that multiple userland goroutines often call write in rapid succession due to concurrent callback paths in the runtime. Single-threaded serialization at the emitter gave much cleaner writes.
- TLS record batching: OpenSSL/TLS stacks sometimes emitted many small TLS records despite large userland writes (due to internal BIO buffering); moving to explicit BIO_write coalescing reduced number of TLS records by ~60%.
- Proxy drain timers were a dominant source of latency amplification: when the proxy accumulated ~32–64KB and waited its drain timer (20–50ms) latency spiked even though backend was producing tokens quickly. Reducing per-stream buffered-bytes and aligning drain timers with expected token pacing reduced amplification.

Recommendations (practical):
1) Add runtime-level coalescing policy with adaptive thresholds: target 2–4KB or 6–10ms for interactive workloads, with automatic fallback to smaller coalesces for high-throughput batched workloads.
2) Keep TCP_NODELAY enabled for low first-byte latency, but pair it with coalescing to avoid creating many tiny packets that push downstream proxies into burst mode.
3) Where supported, leverage kernel pacing (SO_MAX_PACING_RATE) for smoother egress and fewer retransmit spikes under loss.
4) Work with proxy owners to tune per-stream buffer limits and drain-timeouts for streaming inference endpoints; reduce default buffered-bytes for routes that serve low-bandwidth interactive streams.
5) Expose a runtime switch for TLS BIO coalescing to reduce TLS record amplification (helpful for mTLS-heavy enterprise deployments).
6) Add observability: instrument write syscall size and TLS record size histograms in the Console for per-route analysis; add an alert when p999 > baseline and median write size < threshold.

Open questions and next experiments:
- How do the findings translate at scale with real model token latencies (variable token generation times and KV cache hit ratios)? We need a follow-up run with a small LM model producing realistic token size/encoding patterns.
- Interaction with HTTP/3 (QUIC) – packet pacing semantics differ; replicate the same workload over QUIC/proxy path to understand whether proxy buffering becomes less relevant.
- Explore kernel offload (TCP segmentation offload) interactions with our pacing choices on instance types with different NICs.

Appendix: quick run recipe used in CI lab (abbreviated)
1) Start envoy with config: default_buffer_limit=64KB, per_stream_buffer_limit=32KB, drain_timeout=25ms.
2) Backend binary: runtime-stub --emit-interval-ms=5 --token-size-bytes=350 --coalesce-ms=8 --coalesce-bytes=2048 --tcp-nodelay=true \n   (binary built from branch: socket-pacing-experiments).
3) Client: loadgen-go --concurrency=200 --requests=2000 --mode=sequential-streaming --collect-pprof=true.
4) Telemetry: collect tcpdump on client/proxy/backend, kernel tc qdisc stats, eBPF socket trace, and pprof CPU/mem.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working labbook; some of the configs are intentionally coarse to show effect sizes. We should trim the output and formalize an experiment matrix before merging changes into main.
- Diego will follow up with a run against a small Llama-like model on 1/22 and post results in the linked PR.

-- Asha
